summary: Step 7 is acceptable to commit. I re-verified the whole re-review scope independently and found no defect in the shipped code: `with_interpretation_lock` (Tools/semantic_store.ML:2287-2303) is definitionally unchanged by the `uninterruptible_body` edit (thread_attributes.ML:110-111 defines `uninterruptible_body body = uninterruptible (fn run => fn () => body run) ()`), the `local … in … end` hiding is semantics-preserving (repo-wide grep: `interpret_with_parallel'` occurs only at its definition :2335 and its single use :2401; :2198 is an English possessive), the four NONE sites carry the verbatim §12 texts (semantic_store.ML:2455-2462, :2404-2412, interpret_command.ML:150-153, semantic_interpretation_app.ML:115-120), the Python acquire/release ordering matches plan §8.1 (semantic_interpretation.py:406-407), and every plan citation resolves (thread_attributes.ML:21 is the `uninterruptible_body` signature entry; isabelle_thread.ML:186 is the `uninterruptible_body` line of `try_finally`; schedule_dag uses the same form at semantic_store.ML:1969). I reproduced the suite myself: 399 passed, 16 failed — exactly the pre-existing set named in SCOPE.md; `test_interpretation_lock.py` alone 7 passed. All four findings survive, all minor and all confined to Test/Interpretation_Lock_Test.thy; they are mechanical and need no re-review, but should land before the commit. Crucially I MEASURED the race that findings 1 and 2 assert: it does not fire. A faithful model of rpc.py's teardown (background reader task → asyncio.Queue → handle_client → synchronous close() running on_close) driven with close-A-then-immediately-acquire-on-B gave 600 grants / 0 refusals over 300 rounds, under both an idle and a deliberately churning event loop. The mechanism is that `close(A)` appends A's epoll item to the ready list before `write(B)` appends B's, asyncio's ready queue is FIFO so A's wake-up chain stays one hop ahead of B's at every level, and `close()` → `release` has no await in it; the only path that could delay A's teardown is the 3 s grace period at rpc.py:347-367, which requires a func_task in flight on A and cannot apply to the lock connection, which is idle after `try_acquire` returns. So the three unbounded acquires are not a live flake — what remains is a file that states a rule at :23-26 and breaks it at three of five sites, plus a plan sentence at SEMANTIC_CHANGE_GATE_PLAN.md:613-615 ("the ML test waits within a bound") that is false of those three. That is a real consistency/elegance defect worth three lines, not a correctness emergency; the implementer should not over-react by padding waits elsewhere.

rulings.title: Three acquires in the ML test are the "acquire immediately after a run returns" the file and the plan say may be refused -- only two of five are bounded
rulings.rationale: The factual core is verified. Test/Interpretation_Lock_Test.thy:23-26 states the rule ("'Free again' is therefore 'free within a bound', never 'free on the next call'"), and :42, :52 and :79 are bare `with_interpretation_lock` calls asserted to succeed immediately after this theory's own previous release. The release really is fire-and-forget on the ML side: the finaliser calls `close_connection` (semantic_store.ML:2300-2302), which is only `BinIO.StreamIO.closeOut cout; BinIO.StreamIO.closeIn (!cin)` (Isabelle_RPC/Tools/RPC.ML:353-357), and the `release` closure runs from `handle_client`'s `finally` → `Connection.close()` (rpc.py:402-404, close() at :244-257). SEMANTIC_CHANGE_GATE_PLAN.md:613-615 then claims "(the ML test waits within a bound)", which is true of :59 and :103 and false of :42, :52 and :79 -- a concrete plan/code disagreement, which is reportable. I downgrade the severity from the claimed major because I measured the race rather than assuming it. Modelling rpc.py's real teardown shape (background reader task → asyncio.Queue → handle_client → synchronous close() running on_close) and driving it with close-A-then-immediately-acquire-on-B, I got 600 grants and 0 refusals over 300 rounds, both with an idle loop and with the loop deliberately kept busy so both events land in one ready-list pass. The mechanism explains it: `close(A)` appends A's epoll item before `write(B)` appends B's, asyncio's ready queue is FIFO so A's chain stays one hop ahead at every level, and `close()` → `release` contains no await. The one asyncio path that could delay A's teardown is the 3 s grace period at rpc.py:347-367, which needs a func_task in flight on A; the lock connection is idle after `try_acquire` returns, so it cannot apply. So this is not a flaky test -- it is a file that states an invariant and violates it at three of five sites, plus a false sentence in the plan. The project's elegance rule ("a shape that makes an invariant impossible to violate beats one that asks people to remember it") settles the direction, and the fix is three lines. Note that the opposite repair -- deleting `free_within` because the bound is unnecessary -- is not available to me: it would re-open first-review ruling ml-S7-ML-1.
rulings.fix: Generalise the existing helper instead of adding a second shape: `fun lock_within secs body` retries `Semantic_Store.with_interpretation_lock body` against a deadline computed once (exactly the loop at :27-36) and returns its `'a option`; then `fun free_within secs = is_some (lock_within secs (fn () => ()))`. Route every acquire that is asserted to succeed through it: :41 and :42 (`lock_within 5 (fn () => 1)` / `(fn () => 2)`), :52 (the OUTER acquire only), and :79 (the holder's body). Retrying is safe at each: the body runs only when the lock was actually taken, so a retry of :52's body re-runs an idempotent check and a retry of :79's body re-sleeps only after a genuine grant. The nested acquire at :53 and the refusal at :95 must stay bare single tries -- they are the behaviour under test. With that done the plan sentence at SEMANTIC_CHANGE_GATE_PLAN.md:613-615 becomes true as written, so the plan needs no edit.

rulings.title: The rewritten theory still asserts "free on the next call" at three acquires -- the very thing its own comment says is not guaranteed
rulings.rationale: Same finding as mltest-ml-S7-RR-1, independently reached and with the same sites (:42, :52, :79) and the same evidence chain (semantic_store.ML:2300-2302 → RPC.ML:353-356 → rpc.py:402-404 → semantic_interpretation.py:407-412). Its own hedge -- "the window is narrow because the next acquire usually has to build a fresh connection" -- understates the case: I measured it at 0 refusals in 300 rounds even in the tightest shape, where the second connection already exists and only a write is needed. Ruled fix for the same reasons and closed by the same single edit; the two findings must not be fixed twice.
rulings.fix: No separate work: apply the `lock_within` generalisation described under mltest-ml-S7-RR-1, which covers :41, :42, :52 and :79 and leaves the deliberate bare tries at :53 and :95 alone.

rulings.title: Block 4 states the "deadline computed once" invariant twice in two different shapes, and upholds it in one of them only by a hand-placed `val` plus a prose comment
rulings.rationale: Verified on the library and on the file. The invariant is real: `Synchronized.timed_access` evaluates `time_limit x` afresh inside its recursive `try_change` (synchronized.ML:73-87), and `Multithreading.sync_wait` hands it to `Thread.ConditionVar.waitUntil (cond, lock, t)` (multithreading.ML:64-67), i.e. an ABSOLUTE time -- so a constant deadline bounds the total wait while an inlined `fn _ => SOME (Time.now () + ...)` would renew it on every wakeup. The sharp point is the asymmetry the challenger identified: `await_change` (:91-93) takes a `Time.time`, so it cannot renew -- it is safe by its type -- while the second wait (:97-101) writes `Synchronized.timed_access state (K (SOME deadline))` out by hand, re-exposing the `time_limit` FUNCTION argument, and is kept correct only by the reader noticing the `val deadline` at :97 sitting outside the call plus the comment at :89-90 instructing the next editor not to inline it. The file already owns the shape that makes the mistake unwritable and then declines to use it at the second site. This is the project's elegance rule verbatim -- a shape that makes an invariant impossible to violate beats one that asks people to remember it -- so it is not a style remark. Both current waits are correct as written; this is about the shape, which is why it is minor.
rulings.fix: Collapse :91-93 and the inline call at :97-101 into one helper parameterised by SECONDS, not by a deadline, so the deadline is computed inside and nothing outside can renew a bound: `fun await secs pred = let val deadline = Time.now () + Time.fromSeconds secs in Synchronized.timed_access state (K (SOME deadline)) (fn s => if pred s then SOME (s, s) else NONE) end`. Then `await 20 (fn Not_started => false | _ => true)` and `await 10 (fn Done _ => true | _ => false)`. The comment at :89-90 shrinks to one line on the helper.

rulings.title: Block 4 computes a four-way holder diagnosis and then throws it away in bare assertions
rulings.rationale: Verified. :83-87 classifies the holder's outcome four ways (`Done "finished" | "refused" | "interrupted" | "failed"`), and its only two consumers, :94 and :98-101, are bare `\<^assert>`. I confirmed against the distribution that `\<^assert>` is an inline antiquotation expanding to `(fn b => if b then () else raise General.Fail "Assertion failed")` (src/Pure/ML/ml_antiquotations.ML:22-23): no payload, no observed value. So on a failure of this theory in a batch build of Test/ROOT -- which is where a reader who did not write it will meet it -- "the holder was refused the lock", "the holder's body raised", and "the holder produced nothing within the 10 s bound" (NONE) are indistinguishable, even though the test went to the trouble of computing exactly that distinction. The classification exists for diagnosis and reaches nobody. The same file already demonstrates the better shape at :54-55, where a failure names its reason. This is a diagnostics defect, not a comment request, and the repair is a two-line `string_of` plus two cases -- but it is modest, hence minor.
rulings.fix: Follow :54-55. Add a small `fun str_of (SOME Holding) = "holding" | str_of (SOME (Done s)) = "done: " ^ s | str_of (SOME Not_started) = "not started" | str_of NONE = "nothing within the bound"`, then replace the two bare asserts with cases that name what was seen: `(case await 20 ... of SOME Holding => () | other => error ("lock holder never reached the lock body: " ^ str_of other))` and likewise for the post-interrupt wait (`... | other => error ("lock holder outcome: " ^ str_of other)`). This folds naturally into the same rewrite as mltest-ml-S7-RR-2, since both touch :89-101.
